newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia eyes May NATO deal, opposes force build-up.
newsitem.headline: Russia eyes May NATO deal, opposes force build-up.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Wednesday Moscow still hoped to sign a deal on a new partnership with NATO on May 27, but again opposed any military build-up in any new members of the alliance.

Primakov set out Russia's position at talks in Moscow with U.S. Undersecretary of State Strobe Talbott, paving the way for meetings with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana on May 6.

The meetings are considered vital if Russia and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation are to agree terms for a new partnership, intended to guarantee peace in Europe, by the May 27 target date set by President Boris Yeltsin.

"The Russian side is pursuing the task set by the Russian president of preparing a full-scale binding document, hopefully by May 27," a Russian Foreign Ministry statement said after Primakov met Talbott.

"The minister explained that, for this, it is necessary to make more concrete the decisions made at the Russian-U.S. summit in Helsinki on not moving the NATO military infrastructure and on adapting the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty."
Russia bitterly opposes NATO's plans to take in countries from eastern and central Europe, saying this would threaten its security and open new divisions in Europe.

But Yeltsin signalled at last month's Helsinki summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton that he realised Moscow could not block NATO enlargement and wanted to agree a new partnership with it before it starts issuing membership invitations in July.
Despite this, NATO diplomats say Moscow has taken a tough line at negotiatons on the partnership deal to try to win as many concessions as possible.

One stumbling block has been Russia's demand for commitments that new members will not upgrade their military facilities to bring them into line with other NATO countries, and that the alliance will not post nuclear weapons on their soil.
Moscow has also been demanding clear progress towards changing the 1990 CFE treaty, which sets limits on the number and displacement of conventional arms and troops in Europe.
The Foreign Ministry statement did not say if any new proposals had been made at Wednesday's talks.

"There was a detailed conversation. Our arguments on this problem were set out. On their side, the U.S. undersecretary of state informed the Russian minister about the approaches Washington is now thinking about," it said.
Albright, who last visited Moscow in March, has said she also hopes the NATO-Russia agreement will be ready for signing in May but that NATO expansion will proceed with or without it.
She said last week her mission in Moscow was to address outstanding differences with Moscow, including the demands for restrictions on the build-up of forces in new NATO members.

"Russia would... like us to make absolute commitments in the (proposed Russia-NATO) charter about the deployment of nuclear and conventional forces on the territory's new members," she told the Senate Armed Services Committee.
"But we will not compromise on this issue," she said.
